clue.text: Become annoyingly amorous — we object going: " ______ "

definitions.text: Become annoyingly amorous — we object going: " ______ "

parts.note: to become cross is to get cross, so become means get

indicators.note: annoyingly suggests the letters are messed about, signalling a rearrangement
going means leaving, so these letters depart from the word before

parts.note: we as a grammatical object is us

explanation.surface: A couple's public canoodling irritates onlookers, who protest with a familiar line.
explanation.walkthrough: 'annoyingly' rearranges AMOR, what is left of 'amorous' once US ('we' in the object case) is 'going'. The blank is the very remark the clue describes, so the whole clue serves as definition.
explanation.definitionFit: This is the stock idiom bystanders snap at a couple whose kissing in public has become too much.

clue.text: Blasted cat's bitten tot — that's upsetting

indicators.note: upsetting in a down clue means turning upside down, so read bottom to top
bitten means the cat's mouth closes around the next piece

parts.note: mog is British slang for a cat
to tot up is to add

explanation.surface: A wretched cat has bitten a child, which is distressing.
explanation.walkthrough: 'tot' looks like a toddler but means tot up. 'bitten' puts the sum inside the cat, and 'that's upsetting' turns the result upside down in this down light.
explanation.definitionFit: Both are mild curse words used as intensifying adjectives, like damned.

clue.text: Juicy piece of news — time it proved effective

parts.note: brakes that take hold are said to have bit

explanation.surface: A tasty bit of gossip arrives just at the right time.
explanation.definitionFit: A choice morsel, especially a tasty item of gossip or information.

clue.text: Narrator describes sport he wants you to join

indicators.note: describes means draws a line around, so it encloses the next letters

parts.note: one who recites a story is a reciter
RU is short for rugby union

explanation.surface: A storyteller talks about a sport he is keen for you to take up.
explanation.walkthrough: 'describes' is used in the geometric sense of drawing a line round something, so the narrator encloses the sport.
explanation.definitionFit: Someone who enlists new members for an army or firm wants people to sign up.

clue.text: Again Emperor's given order — Congress won't be restricted by it

definitions.text: Congress won't be restricted by it

indicators.note: given order means the letters are arranged afresh

explanation.surface: An emperor issues a decree again, and his parliament won't be bound by it.
explanation.walkthrough: 'Congress' looks political but means sexual intercourse, which such an arrangement does not confine to the couple.
explanation.definitionFit: A partnership where both agree that sexual relations with others are allowed.

clue.text: Singer's keeping last of home comforts

indicators.note: keeping means holding something inside, so one piece goes within the other

parts.note: Cher is the American pop singer, plus the possessive S

indicators.note: last of picks only the final letter of the next word

explanation.surface: A vocalist clings to the final touches of domestic luxury.
explanation.walkthrough: 'keeping' puts E, the 'last of home', inside CHER'S.
explanation.definitionFit: To comfort or hearten someone is to raise their spirits, a verb sense of the synonym.

clue.text: On top of one time beauty — she's fascinating

indicators.note: in a down clue, on top of puts one piece above the next

parts.note: an hour is a period of time
the Roman numeral for one

explanation.surface: Once upon a time there was a beauty who enchanted everyone.
explanation.definitionFit: A beautiful young woman, from the virgins promised in the Islamic paradise.

clue.text: Sweetheart's a joy — short but a really good looker

parts.note: the heart of sweet is its middle letter
glee is delight

indicators.note: short cuts the final letter off

parts.note: yet can mean but, as in strange yet true

explanation.surface: A sweetheart is a delight, small but very good looking.
explanation.walkthrough: 'Sweetheart' is the centre of SWEET, E. 'a really good looker' plays on looks: it means sharp vision, not a handsome person.
explanation.definitionFit: Keen sight, the ability to spot fine details, so an excellent watcher.

clue.text: Director Nick has succeeded in style, but not content

indicators.note: has means holds, so the first piece encloses the next

parts.note: to nick or notch is to score

indicators.note: not content means the inner letters are dropped, leaving the outside pair

explanation.surface: A film director called Nick has made it with flair, but is still dissatisfied.
explanation.walkthrough: 'content' looks like happy but means the inside, so 'not content' leaves SE from STYLE.
explanation.definitionFit: Martin Scorsese is the American film director of Taxi Driver and Goodfellas.

clue.text: Removed Dexter, retired hurt

indicators.note: retired means went back, so the name is read backwards

parts.note: Ted Dexter was an England cricket captain
hurt in the sense of felt pain, ached

explanation.surface: A cricketer called Dexter left the field injured, taken out of the game.
explanation.walkthrough: 'retired hurt' is a cricket phrase for a batsman leaving injured; here 'retired' turns TED into DET. Ted Dexter was an England cricket captain of the 1960s.
explanation.definitionFit: Something taken off or separated has been unfastened, a synonym for aloof or unattached as well.

clue.text: Eager to fight Rod and Henry in turn

parts.note: rod is American slang for a pistol

indicators.note: in places one letter within the next word's synonym

parts.note: a turn in a game is a go
H is the symbol for the henry, the unit of inductance

explanation.surface: Two people, Rod and Henry, take turns in some contest.
explanation.walkthrough: 'Rod' looks like a name beside 'Henry', but it is gangster slang for a gun.
explanation.definitionFit: The phrase describes someone overly enthusiastic, especially keen for battle or action.

clue.text: Hard cash? Yes and no

parts.note: it is cash, but paper notes, not hard coins

explanation.surface: A question about ready money gets an equivocal reply.
explanation.walkthrough: Hard cash means actual money, which this is; but it is soft paper that folds, not hard metal coins.
explanation.definitionFit: Banknotes, paper currency that can be creased and put in a wallet.

clue.text: Stop working in centre of Beaune — I'm getting outta here!

indicators.note: in puts one piece within the letters taken from the next word
centre of picks out the middle pair of letters of the town's name

parts.note: a machine that stops working dies

explanation.surface: Something breaks down in the middle of Beaune, a Burgundy wine town, and someone decides to leave.
explanation.walkthrough: 'centre of' takes the middle pair of the six-letter town name; 'in' puts the word for stop working between them.
explanation.definitionFit: A farewell exclamation, borrowed from French, said by someone departing for good.

clue.text: Eat in low spirits, extremely low spirits

indicators.note: in sets the eating word inside the other letters

parts.note: a cow lows, or moos

indicators.note: extremely takes the outermost letters of spirits

parts.note: to eat a meal is to dine

explanation.surface: Someone eats while down in the dumps, very down indeed.
explanation.walkthrough: 'low' and 'spirits' appear twice: the first pair is wordplay (MOO and the ends SS), the second the definition.
explanation.definitionFit: Being given to gloomy, sulky changes of mood is a state of dejection.

clue.text: In replay, clatters dopy old wingers

indicators.note: a replay plays things through again, signalling the letters reworked

explanation.surface: A TV replay shows a clumsy footballer clattering into wide players.
explanation.walkthrough: 'wingers' look like footballers on the flanks; the definition means prehistoric flying creatures.
explanation.definitionFit: Winged reptiles that died out millions of years ago, so ancient creatures with wings.

clue.text: Criticise cold wine scandal?

parts.note: C is the tap abbreviation for cold
Asti is an Italian sparkling wine
-gate is the suffix for a scandal, after Watergate

explanation.surface: A row over chilled wine prompts a scolding.
explanation.definitionFit: To rebuke or reprimand severely, a stronger synonym for censure.

clue.text: Made a mistake — came clean after changing gender

indicators.note: changing gender swaps the female abbreviation for the male one

parts.note: came clean means confessed, fessed up

explanation.surface: Someone owned up to an error after a gender transition.
explanation.walkthrough: 'changing gender' turns F (female) into M (male).
explanation.definitionFit: Informal idiom for having botched or bungled something.

clue.text: Politicians here — most are reportedly not Labour

indicators.note: to labour is to work, so the letters are worked over
reportedly means as heard, so the word is spoken as a letter

parts.note: the word are said aloud is the letter R

explanation.surface: In this assembly, most members are said not to belong to the Labour party.
explanation.walkthrough: 'not Labour' looks like a party label; 'Labour' is the anagram signal for MOST, R (said like 'are') and NOT.
explanation.definitionFit: The Belfast building where the Northern Ireland Assembly sits, a seat of government.

clue.text: Criminal's old mate wrong — 10 isn't being clobbered

parts.note: a former partner is an ex
a tort is a civil wrong in law
the figures one and zero read as the letters I and O

indicators.note: being clobbered means being knocked about, so the letters are rearranged

parts.note: taken as written, without the apostrophe

explanation.surface: A villain's former partner was wronged; ten more get beaten up.
explanation.walkthrough: '10' is read as the letters IO, which with ISNT are rearranged by 'being clobbered' to give IONIST.
explanation.definitionFit: One who obtains money by threats or force is a kind of lawbreaker.

clue.text: Found in Waterstone's, the right book

indicators.note: found in says the letters are located within the words that follow

explanation.surface: The ideal volume can be picked up in Waterstone's bookshop.
explanation.walkthrough: Waterstone's is a British chain of bookshops.
explanation.definitionFit: A book of the Old Testament, named after the Jewish queen of Persia.

clue.text: Nervous performing at the Fringe?

parts.note: an actor who is performing is on stage
the fringe or border of something is its edge

explanation.surface: An actor feels jittery appearing at the Edinburgh Fringe festival.
explanation.walkthrough: The Fringe is the Edinburgh arts festival, here simply a border.
explanation.definitionFit: Tense and anxious, as if teetering at a precipice.

clue.text: Plan succeeded with huge cutting back

parts.note: S is the abbreviation for succeeded in genealogies

indicators.note: back says the following words are read in reverse order

parts.note: mega means enormous
a cutting remark is tart, sharp

explanation.surface: A scheme worked, involving severe budget cuts.
explanation.walkthrough: 'cutting back' looks like reducing spending; 'back' reverses MEGATART into TRATAGEM.
explanation.definitionFit: A cunning scheme or ruse devised to outwit an opponent.

clue.text: Cross, tense and nearly going nuts

parts.note: T is the grammar abbreviation for tense

indicators.note: nuts means crazy, signalling the letters are scrambled
nearly drops the last letter

explanation.surface: Angry, edgy and close to losing one's mind.
explanation.walkthrough: 'Cross' looks like angry but is a noun: a hybrid. 'nearly' cuts GOING to GOIN, rearranged by 'nuts' into IGON.
explanation.definitionFit: A hybrid animal bred from a male tiger and a lioness.

clue.text: Writer's book is out around second half of the month

indicators.note: out puts the two letters on the outside of the book letter

parts.note: taken as written

indicators.note: around turns the following letters back to front
second half of keeps only the last two of the month's four letters

parts.note: the month here is June

explanation.surface: A book is out of print around the end of the month.
explanation.walkthrough: 'out' puts 'is' around the book letter; 'second half of' the month means the end of June, turned 'around'. 'Writer's' is the definition with 's for 'is'.
explanation.definitionFit: Henrik Ibsen, the Norwegian dramatist of A Doll's House, is a celebrated playwright.

clue.text: Flash Gordon, flyer

indicators.note: flash as a twist of the name of the comic-strip hero, signalling rearrangement

explanation.surface: The comic-strip space hero Flash Gordon is a famous flyer.
explanation.walkthrough: Flash Gordon is a whole name, but 'Flash' is the signal to rearrange GORDON.
explanation.definitionFit: A glossy black songbird of Africa, Asia and Australia, so a creature that flies.

clue.text: Has new single out — it's dirty

indicators.note: out puts the single word outside the rearranged letters

parts.note: a single person is unmarried, unwed

indicators.note: new signals the letters remade into a fresh order

explanation.surface: A band releases a new single, and it is filthy.
explanation.walkthrough: 'single out' reads as a record release, but 'single' means unmarried and goes 'out'side the 'new' arrangement of 'Has'.
explanation.definitionFit: Never having been cleaned is a state of being grimy and soiled.

clue.text: Open Dad's wine

parts.note: pa is a familiar word for father
tent is a deep red Spanish wine

explanation.surface: Uncork Father's bottle of wine.
explanation.walkthrough: TENT is an old name for a dark red Spanish wine.
explanation.definitionFit: Plain and obvious, as in a blatant lie; an adjective sense meaning unconcealed.

clue.text: Best saying 12 at start? That's unexpected!

indicators.note: at start puts the farewell word before the footballer's name
saying means spoken, so the farewell is heard rather than spelt

parts.note: the answer to 12 across is a farewell, a goodbye, or bye
George Best was the Manchester United and Northern Ireland footballer

explanation.surface: A footballer saying farewell at the start is a surprise.
explanation.walkthrough: '12' cross-refers to ADIEU, meaning bye, which sounds like BY. George Best was a famous Northern Irish footballer.
explanation.definitionFit: An old-fashioned exclamation of surprise, an oath invoking the saint or king.
